armF.prompt:
Below is a finished English news feature article (already translated from Japanese, no section headings). Write ONE short, natural sentence that captures the core of the story, in a way a listener can understand by hearing it just once.

Requirements:
- Exactly one sentence.
- Understandable on a single listen.
- Do not pack in multiple separate points; focus on the single most important point or twist of the story.
- Do not add any new fact, conclusion, or lesson that is not already stated in the article below.
- Keep who did what to whom, and what exactly it applied to, the same as in the Japanese source article and the Ledger below.

As a rough guide only (Trial-only guidance, not a strict rule): aim for one main clause with at most one subordinate clause, roughly 12-18 words.

Output only the sentence itself, nothing else (no quotation marks, no label like "In one line:", no Markdown heading markup).

[Article]
# A Human Stand-In Behind the Scenes of an AI Service

This story is about human performers behind the scenes of an AI service. In some calls through Meta’s Muse, tests were carried out in which trained contract workers, not AI, made the calls and finished talking with the people they called. It was as if the lead actor quietly changed in the middle of a performance.

What is troubling about this change, though, is not the fact that a person made the calls. It is that the test began with contract workers making calls without a proper explanation. If the performers change out of users’ sight, users should at least be told before the show begins. That seems only natural.

Meta also had concerns that sensitive personal information needed to continue the calls might be shared by mistake with call center contract workers. We should be precise and not overstate this point. It does not mean that a large-scale data leak took place. The concern was that information might unexpectedly reach other people.

A person joining a call may sometimes help the conversation. But if someone else handles information for a task users thought they had left to AI, they should be told who will make the call and who will know what was said. Even when we ask a family member or coworker to take over a call, we think about what to say when the person speaking changes. Services where AI and people work together need the same kind of care.

Meta executives admitted that it was a mistake to begin testing calls by contract workers without a proper explanation. They then put the human concierge feature on hold for now. Muse as a whole was not stopped.

What matters on the stage of an AI service is not only the lead actor’s performance. The audience should also be able to see who is backstage and what information they can access. This change of performers reminds us of that simple point.

[Japanese source article]
AIサービスの舞台裏に、人間の代役

今回の話は、AIサービスの舞台裏に人間の出演者がいた、というもの。MetaのMuseを通じた電話の一部で、AIではなく、訓練を受けた契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを終えるテストが行われていた。舞台の途中で、主役がすっと交代するような展開だ。

ただ、この交代劇で気になるのは、人間が電話をしたこと自体ではない。適切な説明がないまま、契約スタッフが電話をするテストを始めていたことだ。利用者から見えないところで出演者が変わるなら、せめて開演前に教えてほしい。そんなところだろう。

さらにMeta社内では、電話を進めるために必要な、慎重に扱うべき個人的な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフに意図せず共有される可能性があると懸念された。ここは話を盛らずに押さえたい。これは、大規模な情報漏えいが起きたことを意味しない。示されたのは、情報が思いがけず人に届くかもしれないという心配だ。

人が電話に加われば、やり取りを助けられる場合もあるだろう。けれど、AIに任せたつもりの用事で別の人が情報を扱うなら、誰が電話をし、誰が内容を知るのかは説明してほしい。家族や同僚に電話を代わってもらうときも、相手が変われば、話す内容を考える。AIと人が連携するサービスにも、同じ気配りが必要になる。

Metaの幹部は、適切な説明なしに契約スタッフが電話をするテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めた。そして、人間コンシェルジュ機能を当面取り下げた。Muse全体が止まったわけではない。

AIサービスの舞台で大切なのは、主役の演技だけではない。舞台袖に誰がいて、どんな情報に触れるのかも、観客に見えるようにすること。今回の交代劇は、そんな当たり前を改めて教えてくれる。

armR.final_summary: Meta tested human contractors handling some Muse calls without proper disclosure, then paused its human concierge feature.
armR.final_text:
# A Human Stand-In Behind the Scenes of an AI Service

This story is about human performers behind the scenes of an AI service. In some calls through Meta’s Muse, tests were carried out in which trained contract workers, not AI, made the calls and finished talking with the people they called. It was as if the lead actor quietly changed in the middle of a performance.

What is troubling about this change, though, is not the fact that a person made the calls. It is that the test began with contract workers making calls without a proper explanation. If the performers change out of users’ sight, users should at least be told before the show begins. That seems only natural.

Meta also had concerns that sensitive personal information needed to continue the calls might be shared by mistake with call center contract workers. We should be precise and not overstate this point. It does not mean that a large-scale data leak took place. The concern was that information might unexpectedly reach other people.

A person joining a call may sometimes help the conversation. But if someone else handles information for a task users thought they had left to AI, they should be told who will make the call and who will know what was said. Even when we ask a family member or coworker to take over a call, we think about what to say when the person speaking changes. Services where AI and people work together need the same kind of care.

Meta executives admitted that it was a mistake to begin testing calls by contract workers without a proper explanation. They then put the human concierge feature on hold for now. Muse as a whole was not stopped.

What matters on the stage of an AI service is not only the lead actor’s performance. The audience should also be able to see who is backstage and what information they can access. This change of performers reminds us of that simple point.

## In one line
Meta tested human contractors handling some Muse calls without proper disclosure, then paused its human concierge feature.
